description: SAR-Watch uses L-band radar data from the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission to detect and map Earth surface change, even through clouds and at night. I'm an RF/radar engineer (PhD, Northeastern) building an interactive before/after change map with simple "Radar 101" explanations of how microwaves see ice, soil, and forests. Looking for teammates skilled in Python, web apps, or data visualization who want to make radar science easy to understand.
summary: SAR-Watch is an interactive tool that uses L-band radar data from the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission to detect and explain surface change on Mount Rainier, Washington. We compared two NISAR GCOV backscatter products from the same orbit track (July 3 and October 31, 2026) and built a change map that reveals a striking ring of +4 to +6 dB brightening over the mountain's glacier zone. This is the radar signature of the seasonal switch from summer melt to winter freeze: wet melting snow absorbs microwaves and looks dark, while refrozen ice and dry snow let the signal scatter back strongly. The app lets anyone slide between dates, set a change threshold and see how much area changed, and learn the physics through a plain-language "Radar 101" page. Because radar sees through clouds and works at night, this approach can monitor cloudy mountain regions where optical satellites often fail, supporting glacier monitoring, water-resource planning, and hazard awareness on volcanoes like Rainier.
details:
What it does

SAR-Watch turns raw NISAR radar data into an easy-to-understand picture of how Mount Rainier changes between seasons. It has three views: (1) a before/after slider that blends the July and October radar images, (2) a change map with an adjustable threshold that reports the percentage of area that became brighter or darker, and (3) a "Radar 101" page explaining how L-band microwaves interact with ice, snow, soil, and forests.

How it works

1. Data access: Instead of downloading two 7 GB HDF5 files, the tool streams only the Mount Rainier subset directly from NASA's Alaska Satellite Facility cloud using the earthaccess and h5py libraries. This cuts data transfer from about 15 GB to a few hundred MB.

2. Geolocation: The study box (0.3 x 0.2 degrees around the summit) is converted to the products' UTM zone 10N grid with pyproj, giving 10 m pixels (2259 x 2322).

3. Processing: A 7x7 boxcar filter reduces radar speckle, power is converted to decibels, and change = After (dB) - Before (dB) for HH and HV polarizations.

4. Visualization: Streamlit and Matplotlib provide the interactive app.

Key result

At a 3 dB threshold, 7.4% of the study area became brighter (about 39 km2), concentrated in a ring tracing Rainier's glaciers, and 6.8% became darker, mostly on lower forested slopes. Stable features such as a lake look the same on both dates, which supports the processing.

Why it matters

Mountain glaciers are often hidden by clouds, especially in the Pacific Northwest. L-band radar sees through clouds, at night, and through dry snow. Tracking seasonal melt and freeze helps with water-resource planning, glacier health monitoring, and hazard awareness on glacier-covered volcanoes.

Creativity and factors considered

The team brings an RF/microwave engineering background, so the project focuses on explaining the physics (why wet snow absorbs, why dry snow is transparent at 24 cm wavelength) rather than only showing colors. We also report limitations openly: the July product is provisional while the October product is validated, so part of the small darkening at low elevations may be a calibration offset; backscatter change has several possible causes that should be confirmed with optical or field data; and a full 12-day time series would separate seasonal cycles from long-term trends.

Tools

Python, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, Matplotlib, Streamlit, earthaccess, GitHub.

Presentation

Full 12-slide presentation for a general audience: https://github.com/Ut1991/SAR-Watch/blob/main/SAR-Watch_Final_Presentation.pdf

The 30-second demo video narration uses an AI-generated voice (Microsoft Clipchamp text-to-speech), labeled in the video.
